title: Alexander Hilsberg and conductors who pick on players
summary: Hilsberg, a former Philadelphia concertmaster, did not pick on him and greeted players asking if they had practiced; Mazzari then reflects on conductors who stop the orchestra to cover being lost.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: And Alexander Hillsberg. What did you do?

Oh, Alexander Hillsberg. He's conducting the orchestra right now, huh? Well, I played on the Hillsberg full season and then I was only called in as extra strings were needed. But fortunately, uh, I, Hillsberg was one of the conductors who didn't pick on me and we got along real fine together. He, of course, he used to be the concert maister with the Philadelphia orchestra, you know. Fine violinist. And, uh, he has that nice smile, you know, how are you? You know, grin. Have you been practicing this summer? You know, things like that.
Well, give me the full treatment on that, man. Don't go back.
Well, let's see, uh, I can't really think of much. Or rather I'm not in a vain to describe him.
His accent is pretty hard. But they say the, uh, musician comes back. He said one year out of the conservatory and he's coming back in the fall, the one season with the Hillsberg.

Oh, yes. And he would greet the orchestra and he would say, I am very happy to have you again in my orchestra. I've been practicing this summer. We are going to find out if you have been practicing. And, uh, sure enough, if you haven't been, I mean, he raises hell, you know. He can tell? Well, I don't know whether they can tell or whether they just pick on somebody, but they have a knack for, I think, a lot of them stop because they're lost and they have to find an excuse for having stopped the orchestra, you know. And so they just pick out anything. And the first guy they lay their eyes on and that's it. We got a lot of conductors which aren't what they should be. I mean, after, I haven't played in an orchestra for so long, you can tell, especially if you know your part, you've been playing, say you've been playing Beethoven's Fifth for so many years and you just, I got so, I hardly looked at the music. I would just look at the conductor, you know, because I practically knew what was coming next. So you, you get to tell if a conductor really knows what he wants or what he's undecided or what he doesn't know what he's doing or what he's... And I tell you, a lot of them just don't.
